source_read: PMC author manuscript PMC6386176 (NIHMS1003328; final edited form Nat Neurosci 2018;21(9):1161-1170), all sections, Tables 1-3 and figure legends, read in the built-in browser in my own tab on 2026-10-31; figure images not inspected; supplement (Supplementary Tables S1-S12 and Figures S1-S10, including the instrument SNP lists, Table S6 genetic correlations and Table S10 Egger intercepts) not read. The PMC page links an Author Correction (Nat Neurosci 2019;22:1196, doi:10.1038/s41593-019-0402-7, published 5 June 2019), which I read on its PubMed record and at the publisher (HTML): it rewords 'schizophrenia' as 'liability to schizophrenia' or 'schizophrenia risk' (title now ends 'a causal effect of schizophrenia liability') and corrects the genetic correlation from the manuscript's 0.24 to 0.25 (SE 0.03, P = 5.81 x 10^-15). The PMC manuscript text has not been updated and still shows 0.24.

claims.overstatement: None for the figures attributed to this source. Every Pasman figure in the statement and magnitude matches, with the right exposure (genetic liability to lifetime ever use; instruments of 5 genome-wide significant SNPs and of 69 SNPs at p < 10^-5), outcome (schizophrenia, PGC 2014) and adjustment (none beyond the GWAS covariates). Points for the editor: (1) the forward Pasman estimates are given without a unit in the statement and magnitude; they are on the same per-unit-of-log-odds scale as the reverse estimate and Vaucher's 1.08, and the claim should say so. (2) The claim's 'per unit of log odds' is the correct reading but is not the source's own label: Table 3's footnote describes the odds ratios as the odds for lifetime users vs non-users (forward) and for people with vs without a schizophrenia diagnosis (reverse), a description the Author Correction undercuts for the reverse direction (few participants in the cannabis GWAS have a diagnosis; the exposure is liability). The claim should keep its own label and note that the source labels the scale differently. (3) The 69-SNP instrument is below genome-wide significance (p < 10^-5); the claim implies but does not state this. (4) For the reverse direction the claim gives the IVW estimate only; MR-Egger SIMEX was null (1.07, p = 0.81), which the authors attribute to low power. Not an overstatement, because the claim words the reverse result as an association.
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 3 (B, SE): forward 69 SNPs exp(0.091 +/- 1.96 x 0.051) = 1.10 (0.99-1.21), p = 0.074; forward 5 SNPs 1.04 (0.76-1.42), p = 0.805 (printed 0.806; the claim's 0.81 is right); GSMR 74 SNPs exp(0.192) = 1.21 (1.04-1.42), p = 0.016 (printed 0.017); reverse exp(0.151 +/- 1.96 x 0.046) = 1.16 (1.06-1.27), p = 0.001. Same as the claim. Instrument strength (Discussion, 7th paragraph): the cannabis instruments explained 1.12% (69 SNPs) and 0.15% (5 SNPs) of variance in ever use, which matches 'about 1% or less' (1.12% counts as about 1%); the schizophrenia instrument explained 3.38% of liability variance. No F statistic is reported. Editors' F from these figures: about 30 (69 SNPs), 54 (5 SNPs) and 42 (schizophrenia). The variance figures are approximations (Online Methods > Causal association..., 6th paragraph: one SNP's p-value sets the phenotypic variance) using effective sample sizes (130,072 schizophrenia; 180,934 cannabis) that I could not reproduce from the counts in the paper with the stated formula (editors' calculation from the reported prevalences of use: about 151,500 for cannabis; PGC2 with 36,989 cases and 113,075 controls gives about 111,500). The variance explained may therefore be somewhat larger than printed, but stays about 1%. Shared data: exposure GWAS = ICC (35,297; the same consortium that supplied Gage's and Vaucher's instruments) + 23andMe + UK Biobank; outcome = PGC 2014 schizophrenia GWAS, as in Gage. The paper reports no check of sample overlap, which supports 'not independent'. The task file's title is the corrected title; the PMC manuscript carries the original 'a causal influence of schizophrenia'.

anchors.locator: Results > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 1st paragraph; Table 3, IVW row, first two column groups
anchors.extracted: Forward IVW, liability to lifetime cannabis use on schizophrenia: 5 genome-wide significant SNPs (p < 5 x 10^-8), B 0.039, SE 0.158, OR 1.04, p = 0.806; 69 SNPs at p < 10^-5, B 0.091, SE 0.051, OR 1.10 (95% CI 0.99-1.21), p = 0.074, described by the authors as weak, non-significant evidence.

anchors.locator: Table 3, rows Weighted Median, MR-Egger SIMEX, Weighted Mode, GSMR after HEIDI filtering (cannabis-schizophrenia columns), and footnote *
anchors.extracted: Forward sensitivity analyses: 5 SNPs: weighted median 0.95 (p = 0.649), MR-Egger SIMEX 0.96 (p = 0.827), weighted mode 0.92 (p = 0.536), GSMR not run. 69 SNPs: weighted median 1.07 (p = 0.156), MR-Egger SIMEX 1.11 (p = 0.340), weighted mode 1.02 (p = 0.823), GSMR after HEIDI outlier filtering (74 SNPs) B 0.192, SE 0.080, OR 1.21, p = 0.017, the only nominally significant forward estimate.

anchors.locator: Results > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 1st paragraph; Table 3, third column group, and footnote **
anchors.extracted: Reverse direction, liability to schizophrenia (109 genome-wide significant SNPs) on lifetime cannabis use: IVW B 0.151, SE 0.046, OR 1.16 (95% CI 1.06-1.27), p = 0.001; weighted median 1.17 (p = 0.001); MR-Egger SIMEX 1.07 (p = 0.810); weighted mode 1.37 (p = 0.080); GSMR (102 SNPs) 1.27 (p = 5.36 x 10^-10).

anchors.locator: Results > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 2nd paragraph; Online Methods > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors' summary of the four sensitivity analyses: weak evidence for cannabis to schizophrenia and strong evidence for schizophrenia to cannabis, except that MR-Egger SIMEX gave very weak evidence for the reverse direction; with the Egger intercept not different from zero (Supplementary Table S10, not read) they attribute this to low power. I2 (NOME) was 0.7-0.9, so SIMEX-corrected Egger estimates are reported.

anchors.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript); Author Correction, Nat Neurosci 2019;22:1196 (publisher HTML)
anchors.locator: Results > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph; Author Correction, correction text
anchors.extracted: LD score genetic correlation between lifetime cannabis use and schizophrenia printed as rg 0.24 (SE 0.03, p < 0.01) in the manuscript; the Author Correction calls this a typo and gives rg 0.25 (SE 0.03, P = 5.81 x 10^-15), consistent with Supplementary Table 6.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Online Methods > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Variance explained by the instruments: cannabis 1.12% (69 SNPs, p < 10^-5) and 0.15% (5 SNPs, p < 5 x 10^-8); schizophrenia 3.38% of liability (109 SNPs). Approximated from one SNP's p-value with effective sample sizes 130,072 (schizophrenia) and 180,934 (cannabis). No F statistics. Authors: the lack of strong forward evidence may reflect the lower power of the cannabis instruments.

anchors.locator: Online Methods > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Instruments: cannabis 5 SNPs (p < 5 x 10^-8) and 69 SNPs (p < 10^-5) from this GWAS; schizophrenia 109 SNPs (p < 5 x 10^-8) from the 2014 PGC study (ref. 66); pruned at R2 < 0.001 (R2 < 0.05 for GSMR), proxies at R2 >= 0.8, unavailable and palindromic SNPs dropped (Supplementary Table S7, not read).

anchors.locator: Online Methods > Samples, 1st paragraph; Introduction (unheaded, after the Abstract), 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exposure GWAS of 184,765 people of European ancestry: ICC summary statistics (35,297; 16 cohorts; 42.8% had ever used), 23andMe (22,683; 43.2%), UK Biobank (126,785; 22.3%). Outcome: 2014 PGC schizophrenia GWAS. The ICC and PGC data are the same consortia that Gage et al. (2017) and Vaucher et al. (2018) used, cited by Pasman as earlier MR studies; no sample-overlap figure is reported.

anchors.locator: Online Methods > Phenotype and covariates, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Phenotype: self-reported ever use (yes/no), with question wording that differed between samples. Limitations stated: a dichotomous measure that puts people who tried cannabis and people who use it regularly in one group; samples differ in age, prevalence of use and national policy; the 5-SNP forward instrument had limited power.

anchors.locator: Results > Genetic correlations with other traits, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Liability to lifetime use was genetically correlated with 14 of 25 traits after Bonferroni correction, including smoking, alcohol use and dependence, ADHD, schizophrenia, risk taking and openness (positive) and conscientiousness (negative). The top locus, CADM2, is linked elsewhere to risk taking and lower anxiety. The authors suggest that liability to start using cannabis reflects personality, which bears on whether ever-use variants reach schizophrenia only through cannabis.

anchors.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript); Author Correction (publisher HTML)
anchors.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 7th and 10th paragraphs; Author Correction, correction text
anchors.extracted: Authors' reading: weak evidence for an effect of cannabis use on schizophrenia, much stronger evidence for an effect of schizophrenia (liability) on cannabis use, possibly through prodromal symptoms or negative affect leading to use for coping or self-medication; in line with Gage et al. (2017), in contrast with Vaucher et al. (2018), which did not test the reverse direction. The correction says few participants in the cannabis GWAS will have been diagnosed, so the result concerns liability to schizophrenia, not schizophrenia itself.

key_findings.note: Numbers right. Wording: '35 genes in 16 regions, 11 of them not identified by the variant analysis' should say 11 of the regions (the source has 5 regions already found by the SNP analysis plus 11 new regions), not 11 genes.

Confirmed from the text: 14 of 25 traits at p < 0.002, with the traits the text names (smoking, alcohol use and dependence, ADHD, schizophrenia, risk taking, openness, educational attainment positive; conscientiousness negative), and the small cannabis-dependence GWAS (Discussion, 9th paragraph). The rest of the trait-by-trait list comes from the Figure 4 image, which I did not inspect; its counts (11 positive, 3 negative, 11 not significant) add up to the text's 14 of 25.
All values recomputed from B and SE.
Trivial: Table 3 prints the reverse weighted-median OR as 1.17, but exp(0.163) = 1.18.
Editors' F recomputed: 41.7, 29.7, 54.4. The effective sample sizes the paper gives cannot be reproduced from its counts with its formula (see missed), so these F values are approximate.
'Unadjusted' is the card's fair reading: the text names no covariates.
Read the correction myself at the publisher and on PubMed; text and figures match.

reporting_issues.note: Introduction 3rd paragraph (32,330 + 5,627) vs 5th paragraph and Online Methods > Samples (35,297).
Printed as 'p=2.2e-16' for income; 'p<2e-16' for fluid intelligence.
Online Methods > Causal association..., 2nd paragraph, describes two-sample MR as using non-overlapping sets; no overlap figure is given anywhere in the main text.
Ref. 1 does print the review's title with vol. 371, p. 879 and doi 10.1056/NEJMc1407928. I did not consult the project's DOI list.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall, judged for the genetic correlation and the reverse MR, is defensible. The causation claim also cites the forward estimates, for which the card itself says the editors would judge high (weak instruments, risk-taking-linked lead locus CADM2, no multivariable MR). The claim's certainty reasoning should use that split.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor once the 2019 correction is applied (liability, not diagnosis). The Table 3 footnote's reading of the odds ratios as group comparisons remains, as the card lists.

missed: Figure 1 legend (b) says the GWAS test was linear regression, while Online Methods > Statistics > Genome-wide association analyses and meta-analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, say logistic regression and a meta-analysis of log odds ratios. This matters for the MR scale: the per-unit-of-log-odds reading of B assumes log-odds SNP effects.

Online Methods > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 6th paragraph: the effective sample sizes used for variance explained (130,072 schizophrenia; 180,934 cannabis) cannot be reproduced from the paper's counts with its own formula 4/(1/cases + 1/controls). Editors' calculation: about 151,500 for cannabis from the three samples' reported prevalences of use, and about 111,500 for PGC2 with 36,989 cases and 113,075 controls; which schizophrenia release was used is not stated beyond ref. 66. The variance-explained figures (1.12%, 0.15%, 3.38%) are therefore approximate and may be somewhat underestimated, though the cannabis instrument stays at about 1%.
